item.title: SBA Size Standards by NAICS: 2026 Table, Steps & Appeals
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SBA size standards by NAICS code: current caps for 20+ codes, how to pick a code when you span industries, and how it decides set-aside eligibility.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The SBA sets a size standard for each NAICS code. It's the largest your company can be, measured in average annual receipts or in employees, and still count as "small" for a contract classified under that code. To check it, find the 6-digit NAICS code on the solicitation, look that code up in the SBA's Table of Size Standards (the version in effect since March 17, 2023), and compare the cap with your company-wide receipts or headcount, including affiliates (SBA, SBA table). A firm can be small under one code and "other than small" under another. That means the code on each solicitation decides which set-asides you can bid on, not the code you like best.

Which option is right for you?

Start with the question that fits your situation, and open the first page listed in the table.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, not registered yetLook up 3–6 NAICS codes that describe what you actually sell, and choose a primary codeCensus NAICS search
Registered in SAM.gov, bidding regularlyCheck your size against the NAICS code on each solicitation before you write the proposal13 CFR 121.201 size table
Your work spans several industriesRank your codes by the receipts or headcount behind them, and note where you're small and where you aren'tSBA Table of Size Standards (Excel)
Growing fast and close to a capWork out your 5-year receipts average or 24-month employee average now13 CFR 121.104
Tight budget, want a second opinionFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator before you pay anyoneAPEX Accelerators
You think a solicitation has the wrong codeDraft a NAICS code appeal within 10 calendar days13 CFR 121.1103

Why these picks: beginners need accurate codes before anything else. Active bidders lose the most when they misjudge size on a single solicitation. Multi-industry firms are the ones most likely to be small under one code and large under another.

What Are SBA Size Standards by NAICS Code?

SBA size standards by NAICS code set the maximum average annual receipts or employee count a firm can have to be "small" in that industry. The SBA says that size standards "define the largest size a business can be to participate in government contracting programs," and that most manufacturers with 500 or fewer employees and most non-manufacturers with average annual receipts under $7.5 million qualify as small, though many industries have higher limits (SBA).

Each standard is attached to a 6-digit code from the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). The regulation that lists them all is 13 CFR 121.201. The SBA publishes the same data as a PDF and an Excel file. The table version in effect as of October 2026 is dated March 17, 2023 (SBA table page). The SBA counts 995 separate size standards today (Mayer Brown).

Three rules apply to every code:

  • The cap is company-wide. You measure the whole business against the cap, plus every affiliate. The SBA says you "must include the employees or receipts of all affiliates" (SBA). You don't split your revenue by NAICS code.
  • Some codes have exceptions. For example, 541330 Engineering Services has a $25.5 million cap, but its exception for military and aerospace equipment and military weapons is $47.0 million (13 CFR 121.201).
  • Each contract carries one code. The contracting officer assigns one NAICS code and its size standard to each solicitation, contract and order (FAR 19.102).

How to Find Your NAICS Code and Matching Size Standard

First find the NAICS code that best matches each product or service you sell. Then look up that code in the SBA table to get the employee or receipts cap. The SBA notes that a business "will generally have a primary NAICS code, but it can also have multiple NAICS codes if it sells multiple products and services" (SBA).

Step-by-step lookup

  1. Search the Census NAICS tool. Go to census.gov/naics, type a plain keyword into the NAICS search box (for example, "janitorial" or "software"), and choose the 2022 NAICS year. That's the edition behind the current SBA table. Open each result and read the full description, including the "cross-references" that tell you which activities belong somewhere else.
  2. Write down every code that fits real revenue. For each candidate code, ask whether you've actually earned money from that work or can show past performance in it. Leave out codes you're only hoping to grow into.
  3. Get the cap. Download the Excel version of the SBA Table of Size Standards and filter the NAICS column for your codes. The PDF and 13 CFR 121.201 contain the same numbers. Check the footnotes for exceptions.
  4. Run the SBA tool as a cross-check. The SBA Size Standards Tool asks "Do you qualify as a small business for government contracting purposes?" and walks you through code and size inputs. It gives you a quick answer, not a formal determination.
  5. Enter the codes in SAM.gov. In your entity registration, add the codes and choose a primary NAICS. When you select at least one small business code, SAM.gov asks for Size Metrics (receipts and employees) and uses them to show your size status for each code (SAM.gov entity checklist). If you aren't registered yet, follow our SAM.gov registration guide.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Mistake: using a code from your state license or tax return without checking it. Fix: read the Census definition. A code that's close enough for tax purposes can carry a very different cap.
  • Mistake: reading the 4- or 5-digit industry group. Fix: size standards attach to the 6-digit code (and sometimes to an exception under it). Always check all six digits.
  • Mistake: using an old PDF of the table. Fix: confirm that the file name or header says "Effective March 17, 2023," or a later date if the SBA issues a new final rule.

SBA Size Standards by NAICS Code: Employees vs. Revenue Table

Manufacturing and wholesale codes mostly use employee caps. Services, construction and retail codes mostly use average annual receipts. The numbers below come from 13 CFR 121.201 as of October 2026. Check the official page before you bid, because a proposed overhaul is pending (covered below).

Two things in this table catch people out.

Codes that sound alike can have different caps. Electrical contractors (238210) are capped at $19.0 million, while a general contractor on commercial buildings (236220) gets $45.0 million. Engineering (541330) sits $8.5 million below computer systems design (541512).

The ITVAR exception changes the measure entirely. For 541519, an IT value-added reseller is measured by employees (150), not receipts. The exception applies only when value-added services make up at least 15% and no more than 50% of the contract price (13 CFR 121.201).

For supply contracts where you resell rather than manufacture, a firm can still be small with 500 or fewer employees if it meets the nonmanufacturer rule (13 CFR 121.402).

How to Choose the Right NAICS Code When Your Business Spans Multiple Industries

Make your primary NAICS code the activity that brings in the most revenue. Then list every other code you can honestly perform, even where you're too large. You don't pick a contract's code. The contracting officer does. So the real decision is which opportunities you go after and how you present your registration.

Why "choose the most favorable cap" doesn't work

You can't earn a bigger cap by naming a different code as primary. On any solicitation, your size is measured against the code the contracting officer assigned, which is based on "the principal purpose of the product or service being acquired" (13 CFR 121.402). Your SAM.gov primary code matters elsewhere. Several SBA programs check it. Under 13 CFR 121.404, a firm applying to programs such as 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB or SDVOSB must "qualify as small under the size standard corresponding to any NAICS code listed in its SAM profile." Agencies also tend to search SAM by NAICS when they do market research. A primary code that doesn't match your track record leads to mismatched outreach and weaker past-performance stories.

Steps for a multi-industry firm

  1. Split your last 5 fiscal years of revenue by activity. Use your own books, for example invoices tagged by service line. This tells you which activity is really primary.
  2. Calculate one company-wide size figure. Do this once, using the methods in the receipts section below. Your size is the same number no matter which code you test it against.
  3. Compare that number with every code's cap. Put your codes in a simple sheet with three columns: code, cap, and small (yes or no).
  4. Make the highest-revenue activity your primary code. If two activities are close, choose the one where you have the strongest past performance.
  5. Keep every honest code in SAM, including the ones where you're large. You can still compete on full-and-open contracts and act as a subcontractor under those codes. SAM.gov shows your status per code.
  6. Point your set-aside search at the codes where you're small. In SAM.gov Contract Opportunities, filter by NAICS Code and Set Aside, and save searches only for the "yes" codes.

Example (illustrative numbers)

An IT and engineering firm has 5-year average receipts of $28.0 million. It's small under 541512 ($34.0M cap) and other than small under 541330 ($25.5M cap), unless an engineering solicitation uses the military and aerospace exception ($47.0M). The firm makes 541512 its primary code because most of its revenue comes from systems design. It keeps 541330 listed and bids on engineering set-asides only when the solicitation names the $47.0M exception.

Pitfalls

  • Adding codes you can't support. Being listed doesn't make you eligible, and the claim can backfire in a size or responsibility review. Keep to work you've done or can clearly staff.
  • Forgetting that size is tested at the offer. Size is fixed on the date you submit your "initial offer or response which includes price" (13 CFR 121.404). A large year can tip you over just before a big bid. Recalculate before every set-aside proposal.

How NAICS Code Choice Affects Set-Aside Eligibility

The NAICS code on a solicitation decides which size standard applies. So the same firm can be eligible for one set-aside and shut out of another. When you submit a bid on a set-aside, or register as small, you're legally certifying your size (13 CFR 121.108). Read the code before you decide to bid.

Where to read the code

On a SAM.gov opportunity page, look at the Classification block. NAICS Code and Set Aside (or Original Set Aside) are shown together. The solicitation document repeats the code and size standard in its representations and certifications.

Example (illustrative)

A specialty electrical contractor averages $24.0 million in receipts. An agency posts a total small business set-aside under 238210 ($19.0M cap). The firm is other than small and can't bid as a small business. A month later, another agency posts a renovation project as a small business set-aside under 236220 ($45.0M cap). Now the same firm is small. Nothing about the company changed. Only the code changed. If you're still deciding between total and partial set-asides, see our total vs partial set-aside checklist.

Socioeconomic programs use the same test

Size eligibility for SDVOSB, WOSB and 8(a) set-asides also depends on the solicitation's NAICS code. For the program-specific requirements, see our SDVOSB eligibility checklist and our 8(a) pass/fail checklist.

What happens if a competitor thinks you're too big

Any interested offeror can file a size protest. It has to reach the contracting officer by close of business on the 5th business day after bid opening (sealed bids) or after notice of the apparent awardee (negotiated buys). The SBA dismisses protests that arrive late (13 CFR 121.1004). Contracting officers and the SBA aren't bound by that window (13 CFR 121.1004). Keep your receipts and payroll workpapers ready before you bid so you can answer one.

Use sources-sought notices to influence the code

During market research, you can tell the agency which code fits the work and why. A well-argued sources-sought response is the cheapest way to head off a bad code before the solicitation is posted. Our sources sought response template has a spot for this.

SBA NAICS Small Business Size Standards: 2026 Updates

As of October 2026, no new final size standards have taken effect this year. The March 17, 2023 table still applies. In August 2026, though, the SBA proposed a major overhaul. The last inflation adjustment to receipts-based standards was published November 17, 2022, and the SBA adjusts for inflation at least once every five years (Federal Register, Aug. 20, 2026).

What the August 20, 2026 proposal would change

The SBA published a proposed rule (RIN 3245-AI67, docket SBA-2026-0199) and a methodology notice (docket SBA-2026-0265). Comments were due September 21, 2026 (Mayer Brown; Federal Register). The main points:

  • 995 size standards would shrink to 338, mostly at the 4- or 5-digit NAICS level instead of 6 digits.
  • All 18 federal contracting exceptions would be removed.
  • Employee-based standards would become the default (208 of the 338). Receipts-based standards would cover 129, and one would be asset-based.
  • Receipts-based standards would be adjusted for inflation and for productivity growth, using nominal GDP per employee.
  • New minimums would be 500 employees or $30.6 million in receipts (Holland & Knight).
Current code(s)Current standardProposed standardProposed code

541611, 541618, 541690$19M–$24.5M$295M5416
541330$25.5M$252M54133
5417151,000 employees2,800 employees54171
561210$47M$156M5612
513210$47M3,600 employees5132

Source: Mayer Brown summary of the proposed rule.

The SBA estimates that about 114,541 more firms would qualify as small, including 37,002 current federal contractors holding about $71 billion in FY2025 obligations (Mayer Brown).

What this means for you right now

  • Bid on today's numbers. "Current size standards remain in effect unless and until final rules are issued" (Mayer Brown). If you certify under a proposed cap, you're misrepresenting your size.
  • If you're small today, plan for more competition. If the proposal is finalized as drafted, much larger firms would be eligible for the same set-asides.
  • Watch the NAICS edition too. OMB asked for comments on proposed NAICS 2027 updates on July 13, 2026 (Federal Register). The SBA usually adopts new NAICS editions in its size standards, so some codes may be renumbered later.
  • After any final rule, update SAM.gov. When the 2023 table took effect, the SBA reminded firms that they "must update their SAM registration in order to have their small business status updated" (SBA table page).

How to Calculate Average Annual Receipts for Size Standard Purposes

Average annual receipts are your total receipts over the last 5 completed fiscal years, divided by 5. The few exclusions are listed in 13 CFR 121.104. The SBA's plain-language version: total income plus cost of goods sold from your federal tax returns, averaged over the latest five complete fiscal years (SBA).

Steps

  1. Pull your last 5 filed returns. Use completed fiscal years only. The year in progress doesn't count.
  2. For each year, add total income and cost of goods sold as reported on the return.
  3. Subtract only the allowed exclusions: net capital gains or losses, taxes collected and remitted to a taxing authority, proceeds from transactions between affiliates, and amounts collected for another party by travel agents, real estate agents, advertising agencies, freight forwarders and customs brokers. The rule says these "are the only exclusions" (13 CFR 121.104). Pass-through subcontractor costs aren't on the list, so they stay in.
  4. Add your affiliates' receipts for the full period, including those of a firm you acquired partway through. Leave out a former affiliate if the affiliation ended before the date size is determined (13 CFR 121.104).
  5. Divide by 5. If you've been in business less than 5 years, divide total receipts by the number of weeks in business and multiply by 52 (13 CFR 121.104).

Example (illustrative numbers)

Receipts for FY2021–FY2025: $22M, $26M, $30M, $31M, $36M. Total $145M ÷ 5 = $29.0M. Under 541512 ($34.0M) this firm is small. Under 541330 ($25.5M) it isn't. If someone used only the latest year ($36M), they'd wrongly conclude the firm is large for both codes.

Employee-based codes

For employee caps, average the number of employees across all pay periods in the preceding 24 completed calendar months. Part-time and temporary staff count the same as full-time, and workers supplied through PEOs and leasing firms can count too (13 CFR 121.106). For example, a machine shop (332710, 500-employee cap) that peaked at 540 people last summer may still be small if its 24-month average is under 500.

Pitfalls

  • Using net income or "revenue" from a management dashboard. Use the tax-return figures.
  • Counting only the parent entity. Affiliation from ownership, common management or economic dependence pulls other firms' numbers in (see FAQ).

What to Do If You Disagree With a Contract's Assigned NAICS Code

If you think a solicitation's NAICS code is wrong, file a NAICS code appeal with the SBA's Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) within 10 calendar days after the solicitation, or the amendment that changed the code, is issued (13 CFR 121.1103). If you don't appeal in time, the contracting officer's designation is final (FAR 19.102).

Steps

  1. Mark the deadline on day one. Count 10 calendar days from the issue date, weekends included. OHA dismisses appeals that come in late (13 CFR 121.1103).
  2. Ask the contracting officer first. Point out the mismatch in writing, quoting the Census NAICS definition. An amendment fixes things faster than an appeal. Keep the clock in mind while you wait, though.
  3. Build the argument around "principal purpose." Show which component accounts for the largest share of contract value, using the statement of work and the factors in 13 CFR 121.402: the NAICS Manual descriptions, the solicitation's description, and the relative value of the components.
  4. Include the required contents: the solicitation number, the contracting officer's name and contact details, your identifying information, and "a full and specific statement as to why the NAICS code designation is erroneous, and argument in support thereof" (13 CFR 121.1103).
  5. File with OHA. The regulation lists OHA, U.S. Small Business Administration, 409 3rd Street SW, Suite 5900, Washington, DC 20416. Check OHA's current filing instructions before you send it.
  6. Expect the deadline to be paused. When an appeal is received, the contracting officer must stay the date for receipt of offers (13 CFR 121.1103).

Pitfalls

  • Appealing because you want a bigger cap. OHA asks what the government is buying, not which code helps you. Argue from the statement of work.
  • 8(a) sole-source awards. Only the SBA's Associate Administrator for Business Development may appeal those (13 CFR 121.1103).
  • Assuming unrestricted buys can't be appealed. They can. Appeals are allowed whether or not the procurement is reserved for small businesses (13 CFR 121.1103).

Next steps

Do these today:

  1. Download the Excel Table of Size Standards and make a sheet with your codes, their caps, and a yes/no for whether you're small.
  2. Work out your 5-year receipts average (or 24-month employee average) from filed returns and payroll, including affiliates, and save the workpapers.
  3. In SAM.gov Contract Opportunities, save a search filtered by NAICS Code (your "yes" codes only) and Set Aside.

If you'd rather not do this yourself:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) offer no-cost counseling on NAICS selection, SAM.gov and bid preparation (APEX Accelerators). They're a good fit for first-time bidders. They're less useful if you need a legal opinion on affiliation or help with an active protest, because counselors don't represent you.
  • A government contracts attorney is the right call for affiliation questions, a size protest you received, or an OHA appeal. Fees are set by each firm, so ask for a written estimate or flat fee up front (as of October 2026; check with the firm). If your question is just "which code fits my services," an attorney is more than you need.

FAQ

What is the SBA size standard for my industry?

Look up your 6-digit NAICS code in 13 CFR 121.201 or the SBA's March 17, 2023 table. For example, 541511 Custom Computer Programming is $34.0 million in receipts, and 336411 Aircraft Manufacturing is 1,500 employees. Check footnotes for exceptions, such as the $47.0 million exceptions under 541330.

How often does SBA update size standards?

The SBA reviews size standards over multi-year cycles and adjusts monetary standards for inflation at least once every five years. The last adjustment was published November 17, 2022 (Federal Register). A broad overhaul was proposed in August 2026 but isn't final. Today's caps still apply.

Can a business use different NAICS codes for different contracts?

Yes. You can list multiple codes in SAM.gov. On each contract, you're measured against the code the contracting officer assigned, which is one code per contract, or per discrete category on multiple-award contracts (13 CFR 121.402). You can't pick a different code for a contract yourself. The only route is a timely NAICS appeal.

What happens if I misrepresent my size status?

Submitting a bid on a set-aside counts as an affirmative certification of size. Willful misrepresentation can lead to a presumption of loss equal to the full amount spent on the contract, suspension or debarment, False Claims Act liability, and criminal penalties (13 CFR 121.108). Good-faith reliance on an SBA advisory opinion gives you some protection.

How do affiliation rules affect my size standard calculation?

The SBA adds together the receipts or employees of your firm and all its domestic and foreign affiliates. Affiliation can come from 50%+ ownership, common management, family firms that do business with each other, or getting 70% or more of receipts from one other firm over three fiscal years (13 CFR 121.103). What matters is the power to control. It doesn't have to be used.

item.title: SAM.gov Registration Guide: 7 Steps From UEI to Active
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: A SAM.gov registration guide for first-time small business bidders: UEI, entity validation, notarized letter rules, the free process and when to renew.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To register in SAM.gov, sign in with Login.gov and choose Register Entity. Your entity is validated and gets its Unique Entity ID (UEI) during that process. Then you complete Core Data, Assertions, Representations and Certifications, and Points of Contact, and submit. Registration is free. Activation can take up to ten business days after submission, and you have to renew every 365 days to stay active. Most first-time registrants don't need a notarized letter. You need one only to appoint an Entity Administrator on an existing registration that has no administrator.

Which option is right for you?

Choose your path by what you plan to bid on and what state your registration is in now. The table below shows the first action and the first page to open for each case.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner who wants to bid on federal contracts as a primeFull registration, purpose All Awardssam.gov/entity-registration
You only subcontract, and a prime asked for your UEIUnique Entity ID only. You enter just your legal name and physical addresssam.gov/entity-registration
You want grants or loans, not contractsFull registration, purpose Financial Assistance Awards Onlysam.gov/entity-registration
Daily use: already registered, expiration coming upRenew Entity from your Workspace, starting 60 days before expirationsam.gov → Workspace
Entity validation failed or is stuckOne Federal Service Desk ticket with documents attachedfsd.gov
The person who registered left and nobody has admin accessEntity Administrator appointment letterfsd.gov
Zero budget and you want a person to walk you through itFree APEX Accelerator counselingapexaccelerators.us

Here's why each pick fits:

  • All Awards adds the assertions and contract representations that buyers check. A financial-assistance-only registration does not include them.
  • UEI only is the fastest path. Per SAM.gov, it needs only your legal business name and physical address. You can't win a prime contract with it.
  • Renew Entity at 60 days matches the first reminder email. SAM.gov sends reminders at 60, 30, and 15 days before expiration.
  • APEX Accelerators cost nothing. They help with SAM registration as part of the DoD Office of Small Business Programs network.

What Is SAM.gov Registration?

SAM.gov registration is your entity's record in the System for Award Management. You need an active record to receive federal contracts and most federal assistance awards.

The FAR solicitation provision at 52.204-7 says it directly: "An Offeror is required to be registered in SAM when submitting an offer or quotation and at time of award." A companion clause, 52.204-13, covers keeping the registration current during performance and through final payment. In practice, a contracting officer checks SAM.gov before awarding. If your record isn't active, you can't receive the award, even if your price is best.

SAM.gov offers two levels of record (SAM.gov):

  • Unique Entity ID only. You get a UEI without a full registration. Sub-awardees use this most often when a prime contractor or grantee has to report them.
  • Full entity registration. This is the complete profile with financial details, codes, and certifications. Prime contractors and direct grant recipients need it.

The system has been reorganized several times recently. Between June and September 2025, GSA redesigned the registration screens in four waves. According to a USFCR summary, the data collected stayed the same and only the layout and help text changed. On March 24, 2026, SAM.gov released modernized FAR and DFARS Representations and Certifications. If you follow an older video or PDF, the screens may look different from what you see, but the required information is the same.

SAM.gov is also where set-aside opportunities are posted. Your registration is where you claim small business size and socioeconomic status. If you aren't sure how set-asides work, read Total vs Partial Small Business Set Aside: 2026 Checklist before you choose NAICS codes.

SAM.gov Registration Requirements

You need your exact IRS legal name, a physical address, your EIN (or SSN for sole proprietors), banking details for payments, and NAICS codes. Name mismatches cause the most delays.

Gather these before you sign in.

Identity and tax

  1. Legal business name exactly as the IRS has it. Validation can fail over a single character difference, a period, or a comma (Funding Landscape guide). Copy it from your IRS EIN letter (CP 575 or 147C). Don't use your website or business card.
  2. Physical address. A P.O. box can't replace the physical address.
  3. Date and state of incorporation. The validation step may ask for these.
  4. TIN. This is your EIN, or your SSN if you're a sole proprietor without an EIN. The IRS checks your name and TIN together.

Money

  1. Bank routing and account number for electronic funds transfer, so the government can pay you.

What you sell

  1. NAICS codes for the industries you work in, plus PSC codes if you know them. The NAICS code decides which size standard applies, so it determines whether you count as "small" for a given set-aside.

Account

  1. A Login.gov account for the person registering. SAM.gov sign-in runs through Login.gov.

Optional, depending on your situation

  1. Business documents for manual validation, if the system can't match your entity automatically. GSA accepts Articles of Organization or Incorporation, redacted tax filings, utility bills, bank statements, and similar records that show your legal name and address.
  2. An Entity Administrator letter, only in the cases explained in the step-by-step section below.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • You use a DBA as the legal name. Enter the IRS legal name in the legal name field. Add the DBA in its own field.
  • You registered for a new EIN days ago and the IRS match is rejected. Don't resubmit over and over. Check that the name and EIN match your CP 575 letter exactly, and if the rejection persists, open one Federal Service Desk ticket.
  • Your bank account is in an owner's personal name. Use an account in the business's name so the payment record matches the entity.

How to Get a SAM.gov Registration Number (UEI)

SAM.gov assigns your UEI, the 12-character "registration number," during entity validation, at no cost. The UEI replaced the DUNS number on April 4, 2022.

Federal awards were once tied to Dun & Bradstreet's 9-digit DUNS number. Since April 4, 2022, SAM.gov issues its own identifier: a 12-character alphanumeric code. Registrations that already existed got a UEI automatically. Your UEI does not expire, but your registration does. A UEI on a lapsed registration won't qualify you for an award.

There are two ways to get one:

  1. As part of full registration. Per SAM.gov, "your Unique Entity ID will be assigned during the registration process." This is the right route if you plan to bid as a prime.
  2. UEI only. Choose the UEI-only option and enter your legal business name and physical address. This fits subcontractors, or businesses filling out a prime's supplier form.

For example, a two-person electrical subcontractor whose prime contractor needs a UEI for subcontract reporting can take the UEI-only path today. It can upgrade to a full registration later, when it wants to bid directly.

The UEI is separate from your CAGE code. If you don't have a CAGE code, U.S. entities answer "No" and get one assigned after submission. Non-U.S. entities need an NCAGE code before they start.

To find your UEI later, sign in, open your Workspace, and look at the entity record. It's also on the public entity record if you made it searchable.

Is SAM.gov Registration Free?

Yes. SAM.gov registration, updates, and renewals are free, and the government never asks you to pay for them.

GSA's own fraud bulletin (May 4, 2023) says: "The government will never ask you to pay to register, update your registration, or renew." The Social Security Administration repeated the warning in a January 30, 2026 bulletin: "There is no charge for creating or renewing a SAM account if you use the SAM website." EXIM likewise says getting a UEI, registering, and renewing every year is entirely free.

Official cost (as of October 2026; check the official page): $0 for a UEI, a full registration, updates, and renewals.

Warning signs that a message is not from the government:

  • The sender's domain ends in .com. GSA notes that official emails and websites end in .gov or .mil.
  • It asks for payment by gift card, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer. GSA names these methods as scam signals.
  • It says "your registration expires, pay now." Real SAM.gov reminders tell you to sign in and renew. They never ask for payment.
  • It has a login link that leads to a lookalike Login.gov page. Type sam.gov into your browser yourself. Don't click links in the email.

If you've already paid, or entered your credentials on a fake page, report it to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FTC, as GSA advises. Then change your Login.gov password.

SAM.gov Registration Fee (Third-Party Services)

A "SAM.gov registration fee" is never a government fee. It's a private company charging to help with a free process, and you don't have to buy it.

Private firms sell registration and renewal help. The law allows it, but some firms use official-sounding names or wording that makes their fee look mandatory. The SSA bulletin warns that some companies contact entities "offering to register or renew SAM accounts for a significant fee," and that the services are not required. Since March 2023, an outside firm also can't be your Entity Administrator. It can only get a data-entry role. That means you keep control of your record even if you hire help.

OptionCost (as of October 2026; check the official page)Good forNot forLimitation
Do it yourself on SAM.gov$0Single-owner LLCs and corporations whose IRS name and address are cleanEntities with past name changes, mergers, or mismatched recordsYou handle validation tickets yourself
APEX Accelerator counselor$0 (APEX overview)First-time bidders who want a person to review their entriesPeople who want someone else to do all the data entryCounselors advise; they don't run your account, and wait times depend on your local office
Federal Service Desk (FSD)$0Validation failures and administrator access problemsGeneral strategy questionsGSA says tickets take at least several days and are handled in order received
Paid third-party firmVaries by firm; get a written quoteBusy owners with complex records who value their time over the feeAnyone with a simple record, or on a tight budgetIt can't speed up government validation or processing, and it can't be your Entity Administrator

Pitfall: a paid firm can't make IRS or CAGE validation go faster. All of these options go through the same government queues.

How to Renew Your SAM.gov Registration

Renew by signing in to SAM.gov and choosing Renew Entity from your Workspace before the expiration date. You confirm your entity information, review every section, and submit again.

Registration lasts 365 days. The renewal process has a few separate steps:

  1. Go to sam.gov and sign in through Login.gov with the account that holds the Entity Administrator role.
  2. Open your Workspace and find your entity under Entity Management.
  3. Choose Renew Entity from the actions menu. Renewal is an action you take yourself; nothing renews automatically.
  4. Confirm the legal business name and physical address. If they've changed, the system may send you through entity validation again.
  5. Go through Core Data, Assertions, Representations and Certifications, and Points of Contact. Reps and certs got a new layout on March 24, 2026, with a separate Defense Response module that only entities bidding on or holding DoD-funded work need to complete.
  6. Check banking details, NAICS codes, and points of contact. Fix contacts who have left the company.
  7. Submit, and save the confirmation email.

Common renewal mistakes:

  • Only the departed bookkeeper had admin access. You'll need an Entity Administrator letter, explained below. That takes extra time, so check admin access at least 90 days before expiration.
  • Your NAICS codes are out of date. If you've added a service line, add its code during renewal so your size status shows up for the right set-asides.
  • You sign the reps and certs without reading them. These are certifications to the government. Your size and status claims have to be true for every NAICS code you list.

SAM Gov Registration Renewal Guide: Timing and Deadlines

Start renewing 60 days before expiration, when SAM.gov sends its first reminder. Activation alone can take up to 10 business days.

Here's how the timeline works:

Days before expirationWhat happensWhat you do
90Nothing from SAM.gov yetMake sure someone at your company still has Entity Administrator access
60First reminder emailClick Renew Entity and submit this week
45–60GSA's quick-start guidance recommends starting in this windowIf you haven't submitted yet, do it now
30Second reminderIf you're stuck in validation, open one FSD ticket
15Final reminderYou're now within the possible processing time
0Registration expiresYou can't receive new awards until it's active again

Why 60 days? Processing can take up to ten business days even when everything goes smoothly. Manual entity validation adds its own queue. GSA describes it as "at least several days," and an FSD ticket that gets no reply from you for five days is closed.

For example, say your registration expires December 15 and a proposal is due December 20. If you submit the renewal on December 10, you could miss that bid, because FAR 52.204-7 requires registration when you submit the offer and at award. If you submit around October 16 instead, you have weeks of slack.

Put your expiration date in a shared calendar with two owners, so a single unread inbox can't cause a lapse.

SAM.gov Entity Registration Guide: Step-by-Step Process

New registrations follow seven steps in order: sign in, validate the entity, get your UEI, sort out the administrator letter if needed, fill in the sections, submit, and wait for activation.

Step 1: Create your sign-in

  1. Go to sam.gov. Under Register Your Entity, select Get Started (GSA quick-start steps).
  2. Read the four Before You Get Started steps.
  3. Select Accept for the federal terms. Then sign in with Login.gov, or choose Create An Account if you don't have one.
  4. After sign-in you land in your Workspace.

Pitfall: register with a work email that more than one person can reach, or plan to add a second administrator later. A Login.gov account tied to one employee's personal email leads to access problems later.

Step 2: Start the registration and pick its purpose

  1. In the Entity Management widget, select Get Started.
  2. Select Register Entity.
  3. Choose All Awards if you'll bid on contracts, or Financial Assistance Awards Only for grants and loans only. Select Next.

Choose All Awards if there's any chance you'll bid on contracts. The financial-assistance-only path leaves out the assertions and contract representations that contracting officers need.

Step 3: Validate your entity

Enter your legal business name and physical address exactly as the IRS has them, plus your date and state of incorporation if asked. If the system finds a match, select it and continue.

If there's no match, SAM.gov sends you to the Federal Service Desk. When you do:

  • Open one incident only. GSA says duplicates "slow down the overall process."
  • Attach documents when you create the ticket. Tickets without documents are closed.
  • Use documents that show both your legal name and address, such as Articles of Incorporation, a utility bill, or a bank statement.
  • Reply to FSD within five days, or the ticket may close.

Step 4: Get your UEI

Once validation succeeds, your UEI is assigned (SAM.gov). Write it down. You'll use it on bids, invoices, capability statements, and SBA certification applications.

Step 5: Check whether you need a notarized letter

Most first-time registrants can skip this step. Since June 29, 2018, new or updated registrations don't need an approved notarized Entity Administrator letter on file before activation. A letter is needed to give access to new Entity Administrators on existing registrations where no administrator exists to approve your role request. For example, you'd need one if the founder who registered has left the company.

If you do need one:

  1. Make sure the new administrator already has their own SAM.gov account. The FSD can't process the letter without it.
  2. Download the correct template from fsd.gov. Templates differ by entity type, such as domestic or international.
  3. Name an employee, officer, or board member. Since March 2023, outside firms can't hold the role.
  4. Have it signed by an authorized officer and notarized by a U.S. notary (international entities have different rules). Then upload it to FSD.
  5. Add a backup administrator once you have access.

Step 6: Complete the four sections

  • Core Data: business information, taxpayer information, banking for payments, business types, and CAGE. Answer "No" if you have no CAGE code.
  • Assertions: NAICS and PSC codes, size information, and goods and services.
  • Representations and Certifications: the modernized layout launched in March 2026. Questions use plain-language titles and display answers separately from the full provision text. Complete the Defense Response only if you'll work on DoD-funded contracts.
  • Points of Contact: accountable people with current emails and phone numbers.

If you'll pursue veteran-owned work, read SDVOSB Set Aside Requirements: 2026 Eligibility Checklist before you finish your size and status answers. That way your SAM.gov entries match what you'll later claim with SBA.

Step 7: Submit and wait for "Active"

Submit and save the confirmation. Allow up to ten business days. Behind the scenes, IRS TIN matching and CAGE assignment run in sequence. When the status in your Workspace changes to Active, you can be awarded contracts.

Common mistakes across all steps, with fixes:

  • The registration is "Submitted" for weeks. Check your email for IRS or CAGE rejection notices. Fix the flagged field and submit again. Don't start a second registration.
  • IRS mismatch. Compare the name on your CP 575 or 147C letter character by character with what you entered.
  • The public record is hidden. Opt into public display if you want contracting officers and primes to find you through search.

Next steps

You can finish two or three concrete actions today, even if you don't submit until next week.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Find your IRS EIN letter (CP 575 or 147C) and copy your legal name and address into a text file exactly as printed.
  2. Create or check your Login.gov account using a work email that someone else at the company can reach.
  3. Go to sam.gov/entity-registration and read the Before You Get Started steps. If you're already registered, put your expiration date minus 60 days on a shared calendar.

If you'd rather not do it alone: Your local APEX Accelerator is free (as of October 2026; check the official page). A counselor can review your entries, and APEX offices also help with bidding and certifications. It suits first-time bidders who want a second pair of eyes. It's less suitable if you want someone else to do every step, because you still enter the data yourself. A paid registration firm is the other route. Fees vary by provider, so get a written quote. It can make sense if your records are complex and your time is expensive. Skip it if your IRS name and address are clean, since the government processing time is the same either way and the government part is free.

Related guides on this site:

  • Capability Statement Example: 5 Sections Buyers Read First: put your new UEI and CAGE code where buyers will look for them.
  • Sources Sought Notice: 5-Step Response Template (2026): your first low-effort way to get noticed once you're active.
  • 8(a) Certification Requirements: 2026 Pass/Fail Checklist: an active SAM.gov registration comes before SBA certification.
  • Total vs Partial Small Business Set Aside: 2026 Checklist

FAQ

Is there a SAM gov registration guide PDF?

Yes. GSA publishes quick-start PDFs on fsd.gov, such as the Quick Start Guide for Grants Registrations and a guide for updating entity registrations. Some were written before the 2025 screen redesign and the March 2026 reps-and-certs update, so the button layout may differ. The required data hasn't changed.

How long does SAM.gov registration take to become active?

Plan on up to ten business days after you submit, per EXIM and SAM.gov. Manual entity validation through FSD, IRS mismatches, or CAGE issues can add weeks. Submit well before any proposal deadline.

What happens if my SAM.gov registration expires?

You can't receive new awards until it's active again. FAR 52.204-7 requires registration at the time of offer and award. Your UEI stays the same, but you'll need to complete the renewal and wait for processing again.

Do I need a notarized letter for SAM.gov registration?

Usually not, if it's a new registration. That requirement was dropped for activation on June 29, 2018. You need an Entity Administrator letter when an existing registration has no administrator who can approve a new one.

What is the SAM.gov registration number?

It's your Unique Entity ID: a 12-character alphanumeric code assigned by SAM.gov that replaced the DUNS number on April 4, 2022. It never expires. Your CAGE code is a separate identifier, assigned after you submit.

item.title: SDVOSB Set Aside Requirements: 2026 Eligibility Checklist
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SDVOSB set aside requirements for 2026: the 51% unconditional ownership test, control rules, VetCert certification, and how VA and FAR set-asides differ.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To win an SDVOSB set-aside, your firm has to pass four tests. It must be small under the NAICS code in the solicitation. It must be at least 51% unconditionally and directly owned by one or more service-disabled veterans who live in the United States. Those veterans must also control the company. And SBA must certify the firm through its VetCert program, because self-certification no longer qualifies a firm for these awards (13 CFR 128.200; FAR 19.1405). Before award, the contracting officer checks that you appear in SAM as an SBA-certified SDVOSB. Then they apply the set-aside rules of the buying agency: FAR Subpart 19.14 for most agencies, or VAAR Part 819 for the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Which option is right for you?

Pick your starting point by situation. Most readers fall into one of the five rows below.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time bidder, not yet certifiedGet your SAM.gov registration active, then apply for SDVOSB through VetCertSAM.gov and then MySBA Certifications
Already certified and bidding every weekCheck your certification expiration date and your SAM listing before each offerSBA veteran certification page
You mainly sell to the VARead the VA's order of priority and Rule of Two in VAAR Part 819VAAR Part 819
Tight budget, unsure if you qualifyFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator or Veterans Business Outreach CenterVBOC program
Co-owned with a non-veteranCheck the ownership and control rules before you apply13 CFR 128.202 and 128.203

Here is why each pick comes first. Beginners can't apply to VetCert without an active SAM registration and a UEI. Firms that bid every week lose awards when a lapsed certification goes unnoticed. VA sellers face a different priority order than other agencies. Budget-conscious owners can get the same rule check for free. And co-owned firms are where most denials start.

What Are the SDVOSB Ownership Requirements?

At least 51% of the business must be unconditionally and directly owned by one or more service-disabled veterans. No condition, agreement, or trust can weaken that ownership (13 CFR 128.202).

"Unconditional" means the veteran's ownership is not subject to "any conditions, executory agreements, voting trusts, restrictions on or assignments of voting rights, or other arrangements" that could shift the benefits of ownership to someone else (13 CFR 128.202). "Direct" means the veteran holds the shares or membership interest personally. Ownership through another company or a trust, including an ESOP, does not count. The one exception is a revocable living trust where the qualifying veteran is the grantor, a trustee, and a current beneficiary.

The test also depends on your entity type:

Entity typeWhat the 51% must cover
LLCAt least 51% of each class of member interest
CorporationAt least 51% of all outstanding stock and 51% of each class of voting stock
PartnershipAt least 51% of every class of partnership interest, and a qualifying veteran must be a general partner controlling partnership decisions

Source: 13 CFR 128.202.

The rule also covers profits. Qualifying veterans must receive at least 51% of any profit distribution, in line with their ownership share. SBA ignores community property laws when it measures ownership. So a non-veteran spouse's community property interest does not lower the veteran's percentage on paper.

Steps to check your ownership before you apply

  1. Pull your current operating agreement, bylaws, or partnership agreement, plus every amendment.
  2. List every class of interest (voting, non-voting, preferred). Confirm the veteran holds 51% or more of each class, not just in total.
  3. Look for buy-sell, option, or voting agreements that could move control of the veteran's interest to someone else.
  4. Check the distribution clause. Profits must flow to the veteran in proportion to ownership.

Common pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: A non-veteran investor holds preferred units with a veto over distributions. Fix: Remove the veto or convert the units before applying. Arrangements that move ownership benefits away from the veteran can break the "unconditional" test.
  • Pitfall: You assume a right of first refusal disqualifies you. Fix: It does not, as long as its terms follow normal commercial practice (13 CFR 128.202).
  • Pitfall: The veteran's shares sit in a holding LLC. Fix: Hold them personally or through a qualifying revocable living trust.

Example (illustration only): A veteran owns 60% of an LLC's Class A voting units. A non-veteran partner owns 100% of the Class B economic units. This fails, because the veteran must own 51% of each class.

The rule also protects surviving spouses. If the veteran dies, eligibility continues until the earliest of these: the spouse remarries, the spouse gives up ownership, 10 years pass (if the veteran was rated 100% disabled), or 3 years pass (if the rating was below 100%) (13 CFR 128.202).

What Are the SDVOSB Certification Requirements for 2026?

Since January 1, 2023, SBA certifies SDVOSBs through VetCert. SBA verifies veteran and disability status, ownership, control, and size before the firm can win set-asides at the VA or any other agency (SBA).

The 2021 National Defense Authorization Act moved certification from the VA to SBA as of January 1, 2023 (SBA). To qualify, the firm must be "identified by the VA as a Veteran or Service-Disabled Veteran." It must be small under the size standard for its NAICS code, and it must meet the 51% ownership and control tests (SBA veteran contracting programs). SBA also checks two other things. The firm and its owners cannot have an active exclusion in SAM. They also cannot be delinquent on significant federal debts, such as tax liens or loan defaults, unless they are current on an approved repayment plan (13 CFR 128.201).

Official numbers (as of October 2026; check the official pages)

  • Certification period: 3 years. You can recertify within the 90 calendar days before your eligibility ends. If you miss the date, SBA decertifies the firm, but you can be reinstated if you recertify within 30 days (13 CFR 128.306).
  • Change reporting: Tell SBA about eligibility changes within 30 calendar days (13 CFR 128.306).
  • Processing time: SBA reported in November 2025 that average review time had dropped to 12 days, down from 81 days at the end of 2024, and that the backlog of 2,700+ pending applications was cleared (SBA, Nov. 11, 2025).
  • Reapplying after a denial: Wait 90 calendar days from the decline date (13 CFR 128.305).
  • Help line: 866-SBA-HELP (866-722-4357), or certifications@sba.gov (SBA).

Steps to apply

  1. Make sure your SAM.gov registration is active and that you have your Unique Entity ID (UEI).
  2. Sign in to MySBA Certifications at certifications.sba.gov with your Login.gov account. Create a Login.gov account first if you don't have one.
  3. Choose the Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business certification and work through the ownership, control, and veteran-status sections.
  4. Upload your formation and governing documents, ownership records, and anything else SBA asks for. SBA keeps the minimum document list on its website (13 CFR 128.303). If you're already certified as 8(a) or WOSB, you may be able to reuse those documents.
  5. Watch your email and answer document requests quickly. If you don't respond adequately, SBA can deny the application for that reason (13 CFR 128.302).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • A denial for lack of veteran-status evidence cannot be appealed to SBA's Office of Hearings and Appeals. Other denials can be (13 CFR 128.304). Fix: Settle any discrepancy in your VA records with the VA before you apply.
  • After a denial, update SAM. If you don't appeal, you must update your SAM status within 10 business days of the denial. If you appeal to OHA, update it immediately (13 CFR 128.302).

What Is a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business Set-Aside?

An SDVOSB set-aside is a federal contract that only certified SDVOSBs can bid on. These firms must be majority owned and controlled by veterans with a VA-rated service-connected disability.

The rules sit in FAR Subpart 19.14 for most agencies and in VAAR Part 819 for the VA. A contracting officer can reserve the whole contract for SDVOSBs. If only one capable SDVOSB exists, they can award it sole-source within dollar limits. Under FAR 19.1406, sole-source awards are capped at $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes and $5 million for all other codes, including options. The officer must also find the firm responsible and the price fair and reasonable (FAR 19.1406; caps as of October 2026, check the official page).

Set-asides exist so agencies can meet a statutory goal. The federal government aims to award at least 5% of all federal contracting dollars to SDVOSBs each year (SBA).

Winning a set-aside also brings work-share rules. Under 13 CFR 125.6, on contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold, you may pay no more than the following share of the contract amount to firms that are not similarly situated:

Contract typeMax paid to non-similarly-situated subcontractors
Services (except construction)50%
Supplies50% (cost of materials excluded)
General construction85%
Specialty trade construction75%

"Similarly situated" means other certified SDVOSBs. Example (illustration only): On a $1 million services set-aside, you could pay up to $500,000 to subcontractors that are not SDVOSBs.

What Are SDVOSB Set-Asides and How Do They Work?

Contracting officers use the "Rule of Two." If they reasonably expect offers from two or more eligible SDVOSBs and an award at a fair market price, they can set the contract aside for SDVOSB competition.

FAR 19.1405 states the two conditions: two or more eligible SDVOSB concerns will submit offers, and the award will be made at a fair market price (FAR 19.1405). The same section lists who counts as eligible. An offeror must be "designated in SAM as an SDVOSB concern certified by SBA." The other route is closing out: it covers firms that represented SDVOSB status in SAM and applied to SBA by December 31, 2023, while their application is pending.

The Revolutionary FAR Overhaul is changing Part 19 agency by agency through class deviations. Law firm Holland & Knight's summary of the September 2025 model text says the Rule of Two survives, and that SDVOSB program rules are "substantively the same." One change matters: the old ban on SDVOSB sole-source awards for work already performed under the 8(a) program has been removed (Holland & Knight). For orders under multiple-award contracts, set-asides are now discretionary and can't be protested.

How a contracting officer decides, step by step

  1. Market research. The officer searches the SBA certification database and SAM, and often posts a sources sought notice. Responding to these notices is how you get counted. See our Sources Sought Notice: 5-Step Response Template.
  2. Rule of Two test. Are two or more capable, certified SDVOSBs likely to bid at a fair price?
  3. Set-aside or sole-source decision. If only one SDVOSB is capable and the value is under the FAR 19.1406 cap, a sole-source award is possible.
  4. Eligibility check before award. The officer confirms your SBA certification in SAM and confirms you're small under the solicitation's NAICS code.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: Your capabilities are invisible during market research, so the officer can't find two SDVOSBs. Fix: Keep your SAM profile and your SBA certification profile current, and send a tight capability statement. Our Capability Statement Example shows the sections buyers read first.
  • Pitfall: You're small under your main NAICS code but not under the one in the solicitation. Fix: Check the size standard for each solicitation's code. SBA ties size to the NAICS codes in your SAM profile (13 CFR 128.200).
  • Pitfall: You confuse SDVOSB set-asides with general small business set-asides. Fix: See Total vs Partial Small Business Set Aside: 2026 Checklist for how those work.

How Do SDVOSB Set-Aside Contracts Differ Across Agencies?

VA and non-VA contracts now require the same VetCert certification, but award rules differ. The VA follows VAAR Part 819's "Veterans First" priority order, while other agencies follow FAR Subpart 19.14.

At the VA, SDVOSB set-asides come first in a mandatory sequence. The order is SDVOSBs, then veteran-owned small businesses (VOSBs), then 8(a) or HUBZone, then other small business set-asides (VAAR 819.7005). The VA must set a contract aside when market research gives a "reasonable expectation" of offers from two or more eligible certified firms at a fair and reasonable price that offers the best value (VAAR 819.7006–819.7007). Firms must be "certified and listed in the SBA certification database" both when they submit an offer and at award.

FeatureVA (VAAR Part 819)Other agencies (FAR Subpart 19.14)
Certification requiredSBA VetCert, listed in the SBA database at offer and awardSBA VetCert, designated in SAM (or a pending pre-2024 application)
PrioritySDVOSB first, then VOSB, then other programsNo fixed priority among SDVOSB, 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB
Rule of TwoMandatory, "best value" languageTwo SDVOSBs + fair market price
Sole-source cap$5 million including options$8.5M manufacturing / $5M other
VOSB (non-disabled) set-asidesYesNo

Sources: VAAR Part 819, FAR 19.1405, FAR 19.1406. Dollar caps are as of October 2026; check the official pages.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: You quote a $7 million manufacturing sole-source to the VA because FAR allows $8.5 million. Fix: The VA cap is $5 million, so check which regulation governs the buying agency.
  • Pitfall: Your certification lapses between submitting the offer and the award date at the VA. Fix: Start recertifying as soon as the 90-day window opens.
  • Pitfall: You count on old VA CVE verification. Fix: Certification moved to SBA in 2023, so your listing must be in SBA's system now.

What Control Requirements Must an SDVOSB Meet?

The service-disabled veteran must hold the highest officer position and manage both long-term decisions and daily operations. No non-veteran can actually control the firm or have the power to control it (13 CFR 128.203).

Control is tested separately from ownership, and a firm can own the right percentages and still fail here. The regulation requires a qualifying veteran to "hold the highest officer position in the concern (usually President or Chief Executive Officer)" with managerial experience suited to the business (13 CFR 128.203). Other key points:

  • Time commitment. The veteran cannot hold outside employment that keeps them from giving the firm the time and attention needed to control it.
  • Licenses. The veteran does not need the technical license, such as a contractor's or engineer's license. They do need "ultimate managerial and supervisory control" over the people who hold it.
  • Pay. A non-veteran cannot earn more than the veteran in the top officer role unless the higher pay is commercially reasonable.
  • Board control (corporations). Veterans must control the board of directors, through 100% ownership, 51% or more with voting control, or several veterans with enforceable voting agreements.
  • Permanent and severe disability. If the veteran has a permanent and total disability rating and cannot run daily operations, a spouse or permanent caregiver may exercise control (13 CFR 128.200; 128.203).

Steps to test your control setup

  1. Read your bylaws or operating agreement for supermajority or unanimous-consent clauses. A clause that lets a minority non-veteran owner block ordinary business decisions is a red flag.
  2. Check titles. The veteran should be CEO or President, not "Managing Member" next to a non-veteran "CEO."
  3. Compare compensation. If a non-veteran earns more, write down why that's commercially reasonable.
  4. Map who signs bank documents, bids, and hiring decisions. The veteran should hold final authority.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: A non-veteran co-owner runs operations while the veteran works a full-time job somewhere else. Fix: The veteran needs enough time to control the firm. Reduce the outside work or restructure roles before applying.
  • Pitfall: A key subcontractor or lender has approval rights over company decisions. Fix: Limit outside parties to normal commercial protections.

Example (illustration only): A service-disabled veteran owns 51% of a construction firm, and a non-veteran owns 49% and holds the general contractor license. This can pass if the veteran is President, supervises the license holder, and can't be outvoted on ordinary decisions. It fails if the operating agreement requires the license holder's consent to bid or hire.

SDVOSB Verification vs Self-Certification: What's the Difference?

Self-certification no longer works for SDVOSB set-asides. Firms must be certified by SBA through VetCert. The only carve-out is for firms that applied by December 31, 2023 and are still waiting for a decision.

Before 2023, SDVOSBs selling to agencies other than the VA could simply claim the status in SAM. The VA ran its own verification for its contracts. The 2021 NDAA ended that split. It gave self-certified firms a one-year grace period through January 1, 2024. Firms that applied before that date kept their eligibility until SBA decided (FAR 19.1405).

The 2024 NDAA then extended the certification requirement to subcontracts and to contracts that count toward agency goals. SBA states that all veteran firms "must also be certified by SBA VetCert Program before December 22, 2024." Self-certification remained valid through that deadline for subcontracting and goaling purposes (SBA). Firms that submitted a complete application by December 22, 2024 could keep self-certifying until SBA decided (Smith Currie).

StatusCan win SDVOSB set-aside/sole-source?Counts toward subcontracting goals?
SBA VetCert certifiedYesYes
Applied by Dec 31, 2023, still pendingYes, until SBA decidesYes, until SBA decides
Self-certified only, no applicationNoNo (after the Dec 22, 2024 deadline)

Pitfall and fix

  • Pitfall: Your SAM profile still shows an old SDVOSB self-representation, and you assume you're eligible. Fix: Look up your firm in the SBA certification database. If it isn't listed as certified, apply now. Claiming SDVOSB status you don't hold can lead to protests and penalties under 13 CFR Part 128, Subpart F.

What Is a Federal Set-Aside and How Does SDVOSB Fit In?

A federal set-aside reserves a contract for one category of small business. SDVOSB is one of four SBA socioeconomic programs, alongside 8(a), WOSB, and HUBZone, and each has its own eligibility test.

All four programs require small business status and certification through the SBA Certifications portal (SBA certifications overview).

ProgramCore eligibility testCertifying bodyNotable feature
SDVOSB51% owned and controlled by VA-rated service-disabled veterans living in the U.S.SBA VetCert3-year certification; VA gives it top priority
8(a)Socially and economically disadvantaged owners, 2 years in businessSBA9-year program term
WOSB51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizensSBALimited to industries where women are underrepresented
HUBZoneLocated in a historically underutilized business zone, with residency rules for employeesSBA10% price evaluation preference

Sources: SBA certifications overview; 13 CFR 128.200; 13 CFR 128.306.

A firm can hold more than one certification, and each opens a different pool of set-asides. Example (illustration only): A service-disabled veteran who owns a firm in a HUBZone could compete for SDVOSB and HUBZone set-asides once certified in both. If you're weighing 8(a) as well, our 8(a) Certification Requirements: 2026 Pass/Fail Checklist covers that test. Mentor-protégé joint ventures can also pursue SDVOSB set-asides when the protégé qualifies (SBA).

Next steps

You can do most of the eligibility work today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open your operating agreement or bylaws and check the 51%-of-each-class test and the control clauses against 13 CFR 128.202 and 128.203.
  2. Log in to SAM.gov and confirm your registration is active and your NAICS codes are correct.
  3. Sign in to MySBA Certifications with Login.gov and start the SDVOSB application. If you're already certified, note your recertification date.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (free): These DoD-funded centers offer one-on-one government contracting counseling, including help with SAM registration and certifications, at no cost (Washington APEX). They suit first-time bidders. They are a weaker fit if you need a legal opinion on a complex ownership structure, because counselors don't make eligibility decisions. Wait times vary by center.
  • Veterans Business Outreach Centers (free): SBA's VBOCs offer training and counseling at no cost to veterans, service members, and military spouses (SBA VBOC program). They're good for veterans just starting out. They are less suited to defending a protest.
  • Government contracts attorney (paid): This is the right choice if you have investor agreements, trusts, or a pending denial or protest. Fees vary by firm and aren't set officially, so ask for a written quote before you start (as of October 2026). It's probably more than you need for a simple single-owner LLC.

FAQ

What percentage of a business must a veteran own for SDVOSB?

One or more service-disabled veterans must own at least 51%, unconditionally and directly. For LLCs, that means 51% of each class of membership interest. For corporations, it means 51% of all stock and 51% of each voting class (13 CFR 128.202).

Is self-certification still allowed for SDVOSB contracts?

No. SDVOSB set-asides and sole-source awards require SBA VetCert certification. The exception is firms that applied by December 31, 2023 and are still awaiting a decision (FAR 19.1405). For subcontracting and goaling, self-certification ended December 22, 2024 (SBA).

Do I need VA disability rating proof to qualify as SDVOSB?

Yes. The qualifying owner must be identified by the VA as a service-disabled veteran with a disability rated by the VA (SBA). If SBA denies you for insufficient evidence of veteran status, you can't appeal that to OHA. Fix any VA record problems before you apply (13 CFR 128.304).

Can a non-veteran co-owner control daily operations in an SDVOSB?

No. The veteran must hold the top officer role and control both daily operations and long-term decisions. A non-veteran may hold the technical license if the veteran keeps final supervisory control. The one exception is a veteran with a permanent and total disability, where a spouse or permanent caregiver may control the firm (13 CFR 128.203).

What's the difference between VA and SBA SDVOSB set-aside rules?

Both use the same SBA VetCert certification. The VA must consider SDVOSBs first, then VOSBs, under its Veterans First Rule of Two, and caps sole-source awards at $5 million (VAAR Part 819). Other agencies follow FAR 19.14, which has no fixed priority among programs and sole-source caps of $8.5 million (manufacturing) or $5 million (FAR 19.1406).
